title: JIA-Associated Uveitis: The Silent Threat
summary: Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis (JIA) is the most common systemic association with pediatric chronic anterior uveitis. Often asymptomatic and 'white,' it requires rigorous screening to prevent irreversible vision loss from band keratopathy, cataracts, and glaucoma.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis (JIA) describes a heterogenous group of arthritis of unknown etiology lasting ≥6 weeks in a child <16 years old. In ophthalmology, it is the leading cause of chronic non-granulomatous anterior uveitis in children. Characteristically, the eye is 'white and quiet' despite significant intraocular inflammation (The Silent Uveitis).

sections.title: Uveitis Risk Factors Checklist
content: ANA Positivity: Strongest predictor (Odds Ratio ~8.6)
Age at Onset: Early onset (<4 years old) increases risk
Gender: Females are at significantly higher risk (4:1)
JIA Subtype: Oligoarticular (Persistent or Extended) is high risk
RF Negativity: Uveitis is rare in RF+ polyarticular JIA
Duration: Most uveitis occurs within 4-7 years of joint onset

sections.title: Ocular Examination Findings
content: Anterior Chamber: Chronic cells and flare (SUN grading)
Keratic Precipitates: Small to medium, non-granulomatous
Band Keratopathy: Calcium deposition in Bowman's layer (3 & 9 o'clock)
Posterior Synechiae: Leading to 'cloverleaf' pupil
Cataract: Posterior subcapsular (PSC) due to inflammation/steroids
Glaucoma: Secondary to trabeculitis or peripheral anterior synechiae
Hypotony: Sign of ciliary body membrane or exhaustion

sections.title: Medical Management Algorithm
content: Step 1: Topical Steroids (Pred Forte 1%) - Titrate to control inflammation. Goal: <0.5+ cells.
Step 2: Mydriatics (Atropine/Cyclopentolate) - Prevent/break posterior synechiae.
Step 3: Conventional DMARDs - Methotrexate (MTX) 10-15 mg/m²/week (Standard of care).
Step 4: Biologic DMARDs (Anti-TNFα) - Adalimumab (Humira) or Infliximab (Remicade).
Step 5: Alternative Biologics - Abatacept or Tocilizumab if Anti-TNFα fails.

sections.title: Surgical Intervention Pearls
content: Pre-op Requirement: Eye MUST be quiet (0 cells) for at least 3 months.
Cataract: Lensectomy + Vitrectomy preferred in very young; IOL in older children with well-controlled disease.
Band Keratopathy: Chelation with EDTA 1.5% - 3.0%.
Glaucoma: Often refractory; Ahmed or Baerveldt Glaucoma Drainage Devices (GDD) preferred over trabeculectomy.

sections.title: Critical Red Flags
content: Hypotony (IOP < 5 mmHg): Risk of phthisis bulbi.
Rapidly advancing Band Keratopathy: Sign of chronic poor control.
Secondary Glaucoma: Major cause of irreversible blindness.
Cystoid Macular Edema (CME): Though less common than in adults, can occur.
Steroid Response: Monitoring for steroid-induced ocular hypertension.

rows: Adalimumab + MTX is superior to MTX alone for JIA-uveitis control.
Adalimumab effective in early-onset refractory JIA-uveitis.
Tocilizumab (Anti-IL6) showed limited efficacy in anti-TNF refractory cases.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Flare is not Cells: In chronic JIA, persistent flare (protein leak) is common even when 'quiet.' Treat based on cells, not flare.
The 'White' Eye Trap: Never assume a quiet exterior means a quiet interior; children rarely complain of symptoms.
Methotrexate Dosing: Always supplement with Folic acid (1mg/day) to reduce GI side effects.
Growth Monitoring: Chronic systemic or even intensive topical steroids can stunt growth and cause Cushingoid features.
Multidisciplinary Care: Coordination between Pediatric Ophthalmology and Rheumatology is MANDATORY.
